config.documentTitleFull: WRITTEN REQUEST TO THE OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT ATTORNEY GENERAL TO PREPARE A PETITION FOR EXPUNCTION AFTER COMPLETION OF A CERTIFIED RECOVERY COURT PROGRAMME, UNDER T.C.A. § 40-32-107(e) WITH PROCEDURE AT T.C.A. § 40-32-108

primaryStatutoryAuthority.description: Added in its entirety by Public Chapter 1061 and effective 2026-07-01 with no offence-date limitation. It lets a person who carries one conviction under the driving-under-the-influence section expunge a different, otherwise-eligible offence committed at least ten years after it.

The cumulative conditions: the offence is eligible for expunction under subsection (a)(1) and occurred at least ten years after the conviction; every requirement of the sentence for the offence being expunged is fulfilled; a certified recovery court programme established under title 16 has been successfully completed; no previous grant of expunction under subsection (a), (b), (c) or (e); and not more than one conviction under the driving-under-the-influence section.

A court shall not grant an expunction under the subsection if the offence sought to be expunged involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance. This is an absolute bar even where every other condition is met.
The driving-under-the-influence section. A conviction under it is itself ineligible for expunction and is not what this route reaches.
The office of the district attorney general must prepare the petition and the proposed order and give them to the petitioner to file with the clerk.

The rebuttable presumption reaches only petitioners eligible under the enumerated paragraphs of subsection (a)(1), so a subsection (e) petitioner falls into the bare default and the court weighs the interest of the petitioner against the best interests of justice and public safety.
The certificate that must be attached before an order of expunction may be entered.
Expunction restores the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction.

verificationStatute.description: Notarization is not prescribed by the procedure section and no verification statute exists to cite for a written request. The citation is left null and the silence is recorded in sourceSilences.

counselFlags: The generated artifact is the participant's own written request to the office of the district attorney general, together with the participant's controlled eligibility record. It is not the statutory petition and it is not the proposed order: T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e) requires both of those to be prepared by that office and given to the petitioner to be filed with the clerk. LegalEase does not draft, complete, sign or hold out either instrument as its own, and does not make the district attorney general's legal determination.

This is not official_pdf_fill, because no participant form exists: neither Tennessee state form index publishes an expunction form of any kind, and the state bureau's order form is a court order carrying an approved-for-entry block with signature lines for defence, the district attorney general and the judge. It is not process_guidance either, because a genuine participant-facing written submission exists and its destination, addressee and operative content are all determined.

LegalEase does not obtain the district attorney general's agreement, does not negotiate with that office, does not prepare or sign its petition or proposed order, does not create the certificate or the order the state bureau requires, does not create a clerk certification, makes no judicial finding, certifies no eligibility and promises neither filing nor relief. Refusal, opposition or disputed eligibility routes to an attorney handoff, and the participant still receives the generated request, the controlled factual record and the instructions before that handoff.

The certificate under T.C.A. § 40-32-102(c) is required on this route and an order must not be entered unless it is attached. It is a court instrument completed by court staff; this packet does not generate it, does not complete it and does not assert it has been obtained.

This is a relief-from-the-bar route, not a route that clears a driving-under-the-influence conviction, and reading it the other way would be the single most damaging error available on it. Such a conviction is itself ineligible for expunction, and subsection (e)(3) forbids expunction of any offence that involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance. What subsection (e) does is let a person who carries one such conviction clear a different, otherwise-eligible offence committed at least ten years after it. A participant who wants that conviction cleared is a stop condition.

Subsection (e) is named in neither the rebuttable presumption nor the violence-weighing direction that applies to subsection (d) petitioners, so an (e) petitioner falls into the bare statutory default. The disclosure text for that point is recorded in the pin as not yet drafted or reviewed; the letter states the position without argument.

What document evidences successful completion of a certified recovery court programme, which body issues it, and whether it is participant-facing were not established from the adopted authority chain. The requirement is confirmed; the instrument is not. The enclosure is therefore a bracket the sender fills from whatever the programme gave them.

Recorded open question from the pin: whether a prior expunction granted under subsection (e) bars a later petition under subsection (a), (b) or (c). Subsection (e) bars an (e) petitioner who previously received expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e), but the reciprocal bars in the others do not name (e). The asymmetry is in the enacted text and cannot be resolved from it.

The ten-year interval runs between two events — the conviction and the later offence — rather than from sentence completion. Where it cannot be established from the judgments, self-help stops and the participant is directed to the clerks of both courts.

No fee figure is quoted anywhere in this packet. The clerk's fee applies but the source records no retrievable amount, and the filing-fee field is left null rather than filled with a circulating number.
No indigency or fee-waiver provision appears anywhere in the governing sections. None is asserted and the fee-waiver field is left null.
Notarization is not prescribed by the procedure section and no verification statute exists to cite, so verificationStatute.citation is left null and the request carries an ordinary signature block.

Whether a district attorney general's office will prepare a petition on request, how long it takes, and whether any office publishes its own request form are all unestablished. T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e) makes preparation that office's duty, but no statewide request form is published on any official site and the practice interval is not established. Recorded as a blocked component.

Court timing carried from the pin: the clerk serves the petition on the district attorney general, who may submit recommendations within 60 days with a copy to the petitioner and may file evidence under seal, and the court may not order sooner than 61 days after service. After a denial there is no further petition for at least two years. None of that is asserted in this letter, which precedes the petition.

Recorded open question from the pin: the prior-expunction bars across the subsections of T.C.A. § 40-32-107 are asymmetric on the enacted text and the asymmetry cannot be resolved from it. This packet reports the participant's own answer and states which bars the governing subsection actually contains. It asserts no conclusion about a subsection that is silent and does not tell a participant a route is closed on the strength of a bar the statute does not impose.

Self-help stops and the participant is handed off to an attorney; the participant keeps the generated request, the controlled factual record and the instructions. Eligibility is disputed by the district attorney general's office. That is a contested determination for that office and, on filing, for the court; it is handed off to an attorney rather than argued in the packet. Any other conviction anywhere on the record, including federal and out-of-state convictions that would be ineligible in Tennessee. Handed off to an attorney before anything is sent. Any unpaid court costs, fines, restitution or other assessments, which mean the sentence is not complete. The participant is directed to the convicting court's clerk to resolve the balance before the route reopens. Any borderline offence whose exact section cannot be matched against the current eligible list. Handed off to an attorney. Federal, military, tribal or out-of-state records, immigration consequences and any security-clearance question, each of which is referred out because Tennessee expunction does not reach them. The participant wants the DUI itself expunged. Subsection (e)(3) forbids it. The packet says so plainly and the participant is referred to an attorney if they want that question examined further. The offence being expunged involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, which is an absolute bar under (e)(3) even where every other condition is met. Handed off to an attorney. More than one conviction under T.C.A. § 55-10-401, which closes the route under (e)(1)(E). Handed off to an attorney. The ten-year interval between the DUI conviction and the offence being expunged cannot be established from the judgments. The participant is directed to the clerks of both courts before the route reopens.

correspondence.salutation: To the Office of the District Attorney General for {judicialDistrict}:
bodyParagraphs: My name is {senderName}. I am writing to ask your office to prepare a petition for expunction and a proposed order under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e), so that I can then file them with the clerk of the convicting court under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(a). I am not asking your office to reach any conclusion for me. I am asking it to prepare the instruments the statute assigns to it, and I set out below the facts I rely on so that your office can make its own determination.

The conviction is in {convictingCourt}, in {judicialDistrict}. The case number as I read it from my own record is {docketNumber}. The offence and the exact statutory section as they appear on the judgment are: {offenceAndSection}. My state control number is [STATE CONTROL NUMBER — SENDER READS IT FROM THEIR OWN CRIMINAL HISTORY AND ENTERS IT HERE BEFORE SENDING].

I rely on T.C.A. § 40-32-107(e). I am not asking for a conviction under T.C.A. § 55-10-401 to be expunged, and I understand that subsection (e)(3) forbids expunction of any offence that involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance. What I ask for is expunction of a different, otherwise-eligible offence. My own answers on each condition are: on whether the offence I ask to have expunged involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance — {vehicleSubstance}; on my convictions under that section and their dates — {duiRecord}; on the date of the offence I ask to have expunged — {offenceDate}; on whether it occurred at least ten years after that conviction — {tenYears}; on my completion of a certified recovery court programme established under title 16 — {recoveryCourt}; on whether every fine, restitution amount, court cost and other assessment for the offence being expunged is paid and every term of imprisonment, probation and condition of release completed — {sentenceComplete}; and on whether I have previously been granted expunction under subsection (a), (b), (c) or (e) — {priorExpunction}.

I record what I understand about how the court will approach this. Subsection (e) is named in neither the rebuttable presumption nor the violence-weighing direction that applies to petitioners under subsection (d), so I understand the court weighs my interest against the best interests of justice and public safety without a presumption either way. I make no argument here about how that weighing should come out.

I understand that once your office prepares the petition and the proposed order, I file them with the clerk of the convicting court and pay the appropriate clerk's fee, and that the clerk then serves the petition on your office. I understand that this letter is not the petition, that it starts no statutory clock, and that nothing in it binds your office to my reading of my own record. Please send your written response to my mailing address shown at the top of this letter.

provenance.registryExcerpt: Expunction of one otherwise-eligible offence, with the § 40-32-110 effect. It does not expunge the DUI. A person seeking expunction of an offence that is eligible for expunction under § 40-32-107(a)(1) and that occurred at least ten years after the person's conviction for an offence under T.C.A. § 55-10-401; who has fulfilled all requirements of the sentence for the offence being expunged, including payment of all fines, restitution, court costs and other assessments, completion of any term of imprisonment or probation, and meeting all conditions of supervised or unsupervised release; who has successfully completed a certified recovery court programme established under title 16; who has not previously been granted expunction under subsection (a), (b), (c) or (e); and who has not been convicted under § 55-10-401 more than one time. This is a relief-from-the-DUI-bar route, not a DUI-expunction route, and reading it the other way would be the single most damaging error available on it. A DUI under § 55-10-401 is itself expunction-ineligible and appears in the § 40-32-107(a)(1)(D) misdemeanour exclusion list, and § 40-32-107(e)(3) provides that a court shall not grant an expunction under the subsection if the offence sought to be expunged involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, including but not limited to a violation of § 55-10-401. What subsection (e) does is let a person who carries one DUI conviction expunge a different, otherwise-eligible offence committed at least ten years after it — relief that § 40-32-107(a)(3)(A) would otherwise deny, because that provision requires the offence to have occurred prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence. Public Chapter 1061 Section 3 provides that the act takes effect July 1, 2026, the public welfare requiring it, and — unlike Public Chapter 930 — imposes no offence-date limitation, so it applies on its effective date to qualifying petitioners regardless of when the offence was committed.
